newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RBA has to take wages into account - governor.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RBA has to take wages into account - governor.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of Australia had to take wages into account when forecasting a year ahead, Governor Ian Macfarlane said on Tuesday.
"If you have some information in relation to wages it would be only logical to wait until you can see some of the effects coming through," he told a Sydney Institute function in answer to a question.
He said that recent economic data appeared to show an improvement in the economy and that the RBA saw growth stronger in 1997 than in 1996.
"Our feeling is that some of the effects are coming through," Macfarlane said, referring to the three monetary policy easings in 1996.
Macfarlane said the bank had to make policy changes by looking a year to 18 months ahead and then waiting to see if the the effects of those easings come through as expected.
"Our feeling is that some of the effects are coming through," he said.
He also said economic data in recent months showed an improvement in economic activity, particularly in investment, housing and employment.

"Our feeling is that the sort of information that we have received over the last couple of months are somewhat better than in the second half of 1996 when we were making those (interest rate) easings," Macfarlane said in response to questions from the audience.
"The near-term outlook for inflation is very good and the 1997 outlook for economic activity is also good and we are looking for a stronger 1997 than in 1996," he said.
"And of course in employment, where the growth in employment in the last two quarters of last year was a bit higher than what they were a bit earlier in the year," he said.
The bank also had to take account of data that had effects stretching out over more than a year and a half, he said.

"When we do that of course developments in the wages data form an important part of that, so if you have some important information on this from the market sector or the administered sector then it would be only logical to wait until you saw what the results were," he said.
The Industrial Relations Court (IRC) is currently considering a claim by the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU) to increase wages for the low paid.
The ACTU's 'living wage' claim proposes low paid workers receive an 8.75 percent wage increase in award rates and three A$20 a week 'safety net' increases' over three years.
The government has branded the claim "irresponsible" and the RBA has said the full claim would imply a marked acceleration in wages growth.
